newsitem.title: INDIA: SQUASH-HILL FACES BAN AFTER QUITTING MATCH.
newsitem.headline: SQUASH-HILL FACES BAN AFTER QUITTING MATCH.

text.p: Anthony Hill, only recently returned from a four-month ban from international squash, faces the possibility of another after quitting his first-round match with Egyptian Amir Wagih in the $105,000 Mahindra international on Monday.
The eighth-seeded Australian walked out when the referee awarded a penalty point against him at the start of the third game for throwing his racket.

"Aren't you even going to give me a warning?" Hill demanded of New Zealand official Gavin Whyte. "No warning," said the referee, who was then given a contemptuous gesture with the racket as Hill stormed off.

The angry player had just enough composure to shake hands with his opponent who had already profited from Hill's fretfulness about the refereeing decisions and the irregular contour of one of the walls and had taken an unexpected two-game lead.
The racket-throwing incident had happened on the last point of the second game in which Hill twice had game points to level the match 1-1 but had twice been fortunate not to get a warning.
Once he swore three times, adding: "It's impossible to play squash here," and once he whacked the ball hard at the glass back wall in line with the marker and referee and glared at them.

These incidents may well have influenced Whyte in his decision to penalise Hill for slinging his racket half the length of the court and into the glass wall after losing five points in a row from 14-12 up.

The New Zealander waited till the players had gone off court and returned for the start of the third game, and then announced to Hill that he was 1-0 down before even hitting a ball. The volatile Aussie then decided he had had enough.

Hill will have his behaviour reported to the Professional Squash Association (PSA), the players governing body which is likely to be considering also a report of his part in a controversial match with Pakistan's Zubair Jahan in last month's World Open in Karachi.
If he is deemed to have brought the game into disrepute, or to be guilty of aggravated behaviour, he is likely to accumulate enough disciplinary points in 1996 to get an automatic ban.
The incident led to the disqualification of the fourth-seeded Englishman Chris Walker, who was caught out by the shortening of the time schedule caused by the brevity of the Hill match.
Walker, a World Open semifinalist last month, turned up late for his first round match with Pakistan's Zarak Jahan and now faces a 100 pounds ($160) fine from the PSA.
The third-seeded former titleholder Brett Martin also went out. The Australian, apparently suffering from knee prioblems, gained only 10 points from the Egyptian number four Omar El Borolossy.
